The sūrah's word, denied of the devil, is the word the Book calls decisive, and the decisiveness is the denial's completion.
verses.26:
> So what ˹other˺ path would you take

**The Question With No Answer**

The twenty-sixth verse is the sūrah's turn from the defence to the demand, and the turn is a question. The section has defended the word and the receiver, and now the sūrah addresses the listener directly: so what other path would you take? The question is the sūrah's last word on the argument, and the question is the argument's completion. The sūrah does not answer the question in the verse. The answer is the one the argument has left standing, and the sūrah leaves the listener to supply it. The question's form is the sūrah's form of the closing: the demand stated as a question, and the question with no answer but the one the defence has established. The path is the straight path, and the question is the sūrah's way of making the listener take it.

**The "So" That Carries the Weight**

The particle at the head of the verse is *fa* — the *so* — and the *so* is the sūrah's logic in a single letter. The *so* refers back to everything that precedes it: the defence, the denials, the sight, the fidelity, the outcast denied. The question is not a fresh question. It is the question that follows from the defence, and the following is the *so*'s work. The sūrah's form is the form of the consequence: the ground is laid, and the consequence is stated, and the consequence is the demand. The *so* carries the weight of the section into the question, and the question's weight is the section's weight. The listener is not asked a question in the air. He is asked the question that the argument has built, and the building is the *so*.
verses.27:
> Surely this ˹Quran˺ is only a reminder to the whole world—

**The Book Defined**

The twenty-seventh verse is the sūrah's third movement in a single statement, and the statement is the Book's function. The second section defended the word's origin, and the third section states the word's purpose: the word is a reminder, *dhikr*, and the reminder is for the worlds, *al-ʿālamīn*. The *inna* — the *surely* — is the particle of the settled claim, and the claim is the sūrah's claim about what the word is for. The sūrah has defended the word as the word of the noble messenger, and now it states the word as the reminder to the worlds, and the stating is the sūrah's completion of its account of the word: the origin is defended, and the function is stated, and the function is the sūrah's last word on the word itself.

**To the Worlds**

The object of the reminder is *al-ʿālamīn* — the worlds, and the worlds are the sūrah's opening word made the sūrah's closing object. The sūrah began with the end of the world's order — the sun wrapped, the stars fallen, the mountains moved — and it closes the word's account with the reminder to the worlds, and the worlds are the whole: the human and the jinn, the creation in its full. The scale of the reminder matches the scale of the sūrah's opening: the sūrah that began with the end of the cosmos ends with the reminder for the cosmos, and the match is the sūrah's frame. The reminder is not for a tribe, not for a city, not for the Meccan room. It is for the worlds, and the worlds are the sūrah's first subject and its last object.

**The "Only" That Limits and Lifts**

The particle *ʿin* — the *only* — is the sūrah's word on the reminder's limit, and the limit is the sūrah's doctrine of the message. The reminder is only a reminder: it does not compel, it does not force, it does not drag the hearer to the path by the hand. The reminding is the act, and the hearing is the hearer's, and the *only* states the boundary of the Book's office. The boundary is the limit, and the limit is the lifting: the reminder is addressed to the free creature, and the freedom of the creature is the reminder's condition. The sūrah's *only* is the sūrah's word on the relation between the word and the will, and the relation is the one the sūrah will complete in the verses that follow: the reminder is for all, and the taking is the will's, and the will is the Lord's.

**The Same Sentence, Twice**

The Book states the reminder's object in its standing formula, and the formula returns in the sūrah that opens with the story of the one who turned away. *"It is only a reminder to the whole world"* (12:104) — the same sentence, the reminder and the worlds, in the story of the brother who was denied. And the formula stands in the sūrah of the story of the one who passed by, in its closing statement: *"It is only a reminder to the whole world"* (38:87). The two statements and the sūrah's own stand across the Book on the same sentence, and the sentence is the Book's name for itself: the reminder, to the worlds. The sūrah's twenty-seventh verse is the sentence in its sworn position, the sentence that stands between the defence and the will, and the sentence is the Book's own word on what it is for.
verses.28:
> to whoever of you wills to take the Straight Way

**The Reminder Meets the Will**

The twenty-eighth verse completes the statement the previous verse opened, and the completion is the condition. The reminder is for the worlds, and the worlds' relation to the reminder is the one this verse states: for whoever of you wills to take the straight path. The *shāʾa* — the *willed* — is the verb of the choice, and the choice is the sūrah's word on the reminder's effect. The reminder reaches the worlds, and the reminder's taking is the will's act: the one who wills takes the path, and the one who does not will does not. The sūrah's verse is the reminder's condition, and the condition is the will, and the will is the sūrah's doctrine of the relation between the word and the hearer.

**Istiqāma: The Straight, Continuous**

The verb is *istaqāma* — to take the straight, to go straight, and the verb's form is the form of the continuing. The *istifʿāl* is the form of the seeking and the doing, and the doing is the path walked, not the point reached. The straight way is the *sirat*, the road, and the road is walked in the continuing: the one who takes the straight is the one who keeps taking it, the straightness as the gait, not the destination. The sūrah's verb states the path in its motion, and the motion is the verse's content: the taking is the walking, and the walking is the continuing, and the continuing is the *istiqāma*. The sūrah does not offer the path as a state to be entered. It offers it as the way to be taken, and the taking is the verb's act.

**The "Of You" That Personalizes**

The phrase *min-kum* — of you, from among you — is the sūrah's word on the reminder's address. The reminder is for the worlds, and the worlds' address is the *you*: the one who hears, in the group, the one among the many who is the one the reminder means. The *of you* is the sūrah's personalization, and the personalization is the verse's force: the universal statement lands on the individual, and the individual is the one who wills or does not will. The sūrah's audience was the Meccan room, and the *of you* is the room made the address, and the address is the sūrah's final word on the listener: the reminder is for the worlds, and the worlds are you, and the you is the one who wills.

**The Same Offer, Everywhere**

The Book states the offer in its standing formula, and the formula returns in the sūrah that closes with the reminder and the will. *"Surely this is a reminder. So let whoever wills take the (Right) Way to their Lord"* (76:29) — the reminder and the will, the offer in its two parts, in the sūrah that names the reminder and the way together. And the formula stands in the sūrah that opens with the warning: *"Surely this is a reminder. So let whoever wills take the (Right) Way to their Lord"* (73:19). And it stands in the sūrah that closes with the path: *"That Day is the (ultimate) truth. So let whoever wills take the path leading back to their Lord"* (78:39). The three statements and the sūrah's own stand across the Book on the same offer, and the offer is the reminder for the one who wills, and the willing is the creature's act, and the act is the taking of the way.
verses.29:
> But you cannot will ˹to do so˺, except by the Will of Allah, the Lord of all worlds

**The Close of the Oath and the Sūrah**

The twenty-ninth verse is the sūrah's last word, and the last word is the ground of the will. The previous verse granted the will to the creature, and this verse states the will's ground: the creature does not will except by the Lord's will. The sūrah closes the way it opened: with the worlds. The first verse was the sun, the first of the world's order, and the last is the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of the order, and the sūrah's frame is the world and its Lord, the end of the world in the first section and the Lord of the worlds in the last. The closing verse answers the opening verse: the world's order is stated in the opening, and the world's Lord is stated in the closing, and the closing is the sūrah's completion.

**The Qur'an's Own Formula**

The Book states the relation in its standing formula, and the formula is the sūrah's verse in its parallel. *"But you cannot will (to do so) unless Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"* (76:30) — the same sentence, the creature's will and the Lord's will, the excepting stated in the Book's own repeated form. The sūrah's verse is the formula in its closing position, the formula that stands at the end of the sūrah as it stands at the end of the reminder-sūrahs, and the formula's standing is the Book's way of making the relation a standing doctrine: the creature wills, and the willing is by the Lord, and the by-the-Lord is the formula's excepting. The sūrah's last verse is the Book's own sentence, and the sentence is the sūrah's completion.

**The Frame of the Whole Book**

The last phrase of the sūrah is the phrase that opens the Book's first sūrah: the Lord of the worlds, *Rabb al-ʿālamīn*. The sūrah closes with the Name that the Book's opening sūrah states in its first verse, and the closing is the sūrah's frame made complete. The sūrah began with the world's order — the sun, the stars, the mountains — and it ends with the world's Lord, and the Lord is the Lord of the order the sūrah has described. The sūrah ends where the Book begins, and the ending is the sūrah's last word: the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of the order, the Lord of the reminder and the will.
